claims.text: The proposed alloy is an equiatomic Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA formed by substituting Mo for Nb in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy can form a dual-phase microstructure consisting of coherent B2 nanoscale precipitates in a disordered BCC matrix.
SPS followed by HPT or severe plastic deformation can produce a grain size below 1 μm in the proposed alloy.
SPS followed by HPT or severe plastic deformation promotes B2 precipitation in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The proposed microstructure can deliver yield strength above 1.2 GPa and room-temperature tensile elongation above 10%.
Replacing Nb with Mo and optimizing the Hf/Zr ratio will reduce density by 15-20% relative to HfNbTaTiZr.
Optimizing the Hf/Zr ratio promotes coherent B2 precipitates without inducing brittle phase separation.
A powder-derived refractory alloy can retain oxygen below 0.2 wt% and attain a submicrometer grain size after SPS and HPT.
Coherent B2 precipitates strengthen the alloy through Orowan strengthening and dislocation pinning.
Nanocrystalline grains and coherent interfaces enable multiple slip systems and dislocation cross-slip, thereby improving room-temperature ductility.
Grain boundaries in the proposed microstructure act as dislocation sources and sinks.
Mo substitution maintains solid-solution strengthening while reducing density relative to Nb-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
HfNbTaTiZr exhibits BCC phases, including chemically distinct Nb-Ta-rich and Hf-Zr-rich BCC regions.
The HfNbTaTiZr baseline has density about 11.5 g/cm³, yield strength about 0.8 GPa, and room-temperature ductility below 5%.
The low ductility of baseline HfNbTaTiZr is caused by its brittle BCC structure and high oxygen sensitivity.
The approach is applicable only at 15-25 at% Mo, an Hf/Zr ratio of 0.8-1.2, and oxygen below 0.2 wt%.
The approach is not applicable above 600°C because the B2 phase may decompose.
Vacancy-like misfit defects and dislocations can occur at interfaces between distinct BCC regions in HfNbTaTiZr.
